question: Can a pretrained language model learn a configuration-to-performance scaling law over heterogeneous language-model pretraining logs, extrapolate final loss and complete loss curves to larger model/token scales than those seen in training, and serve as a joint learning-rate and batch-size tuner?

key_findings.claim: NCPL predicts final loss substantially more accurately than configuration-agnostic Chinchilla fits on both heterogeneous Marin logs and controlled StepLaw logs, including the held-out larger-scale regime.
key_findings.evidence: For Marin, the fine-tuned 1.7B NCPL obtains ID/OOD MAE 0.0109/0.0168 and RMSE 0.0169/0.0239, versus 0.0566/0.0240 MAE and 0.0676/0.0326 RMSE for Chinchilla. For StepLaw it obtains ID/OOD MAE 0.0097/0.0223 and RMSE 0.0158/0.0345, versus 0.0704/0.0440 MAE and 0.0949/0.0670 RMSE. Thus the exact OOD MAE reductions relative to the table's Chinchilla baseline are about 30% for Marin and 49% for StepLaw; these exact comparisons are more informative than the paper's aggregate 20-40% headline.

key_findings.claim: The apparent scale extrapolation depends critically on predicting a residual around a separately fitted Chinchilla trend; it is not learned by the language model from raw loss alone.
key_findings.evidence: Removing residual prediction raises Marin OOD MAE from 0.0168 to 0.1503 and RMSE from 0.0239 to 0.1576, and raises StepLaw OOD MAE from 0.0223 to 0.0988 and RMSE from 0.0345 to 0.1134. The baseline is fitted only on training data, using the best run at each (N,D), and the network learns configuration-conditioned corrections to it.

key_findings.claim: Explicit continuous-number embeddings are also important for extrapolation, although less decisive than the analytic residual baseline.
key_findings.evidence: Replacing numerical tokens with ordinary language-model tokenization worsens Marin ID/OOD MAE from 0.0109/0.0168 to 0.0123/0.0217 and StepLaw ID/OOD MAE from 0.0097/0.0223 to 0.0123/0.0357; the corresponding OOD RMSE changes are 0.0239 to 0.0288 and 0.0345 to 0.0428.

key_findings.claim: A single serialized model can return intermediate loss values as well as final loss, but the loss-curve experiment does not establish a uniform benefit from language-model pretraining.
key_findings.evidence: On Marin, fine-tuned NCPL has ID/OOD curve MAE 0.0252/0.0363 and RMSE 0.0475/0.0644. On StepLaw it has 0.0278/0.0415 MAE and 0.0981/0.1696 RMSE. Yet on StepLaw OOD, scratch 135M has lower curve MAE (0.0376), scratch 1.7B has 0.0384, and fine-tuning wins neither comparison; the StepLaw 135M scratch model also beats fine-tuned 1.7B on final-loss ID and OOD MAE.

key_findings.claim: The language-model backbone is most useful on the heterogeneous Marin corpus; on the more regular StepLaw corpus, small scratch and tabular baselines are highly competitive.
key_findings.evidence: For Marin OOD final loss, fine-tuned 1.7B MAE 0.0168 improves over scratch 1.7B 0.0207, scratch 135M 0.0266, and XGBoost 0.0325. For StepLaw, scratch 135M is best in ID MAE/RMSE (0.0082/0.0147) and OOD MAE/RMSE (0.0199/0.0284), ahead of fine-tuned 1.7B (0.0097/0.0158 and 0.0223/0.0345); XGBoost remains close at 0.0095/0.0162 and 0.0246/0.0332.

key_findings.claim: NCPL recovers a qualitative optimizer-by-weight-decay interaction in a larger held-out Marin setting, but this is predictive association within logged regimes rather than causal discovery.
key_findings.evidence: At N=520M and D=10B, the predicted surface shows Lion improving as weight decay reaches 0.4 or above while AdamW degrades, matching the observed interaction. The inputs include optimizer identity, source identity, and the logged configuration, and no randomized intervention or unseen-optimizer test is performed.

key_findings.claim: The surrogate can approximately recover learning-rate and batch-size optima over the evaluated grid, including larger-scale examples, but the paper does not report a prospective end-to-end tuning trial or exact regret table.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 5 places NCPL-selected optima near the exhaustive-search minima and near StepLaw's explicit scaling-law choices across ID and OOD examples. The plotted ground-truth surfaces are themselves RBF-interpolated and Gaussian-smoothed from scattered observations, and the displayed optimum is obtained by a local quadratic fit to points within 1% of the predicted minimum rather than by training the selected configuration prospectively.

anchors.section: Appendix A.2 / Surface visualization and optimum fitting

key_findings.claim: At the farthest displayed scale, the model selects too large a learning rate and can overpredict loss because both the learned correction and the analytic anchor are biased.
key_findings.evidence: For the N=1.073B, D=57B example, the authors attribute the large selected learning rate to training data dominated by smaller models. Appendix B further shows cases in which the Chinchilla baseline already predicts loss above the observed value and adding NCPL's positive residual inflates the error rather than correcting it.

key_findings.claim: The evaluation is scale-held-out but not project-, dataset-, architecture-, or optimizer-held-out.
key_findings.evidence: All 5,130 retained runs come from Marin (2,549) or StepLaw (2,581); training contains models at or below 430M parameters and OOD validation contains larger models from the same two projects, up to about 1.2B parameters and roughly ten times training compute. A source tag is part of the serialized input, and the paper explicitly says it cannot extrapolate to novel architectures or datasets.

method.core_idea: Serialize a complete pretraining configuration as text, replace continuous values with learned numerical embeddings, and fine-tune a pretrained autoregressive language model to predict the configuration-dependent residual around a conventional parameter-data scaling law.
method.mechanism: NCPL uses Qwen3-1.7B as a regressor. Categorical and textual fields use the language model's normal tokens, each numerical value passes through a two-layer MLP, and a scalar head reads the final token. A Chinchilla law is fitted on training-only best runs at each (N,D); the network predicts the residual for final loss or for loss at a queried training step. Training first updates the numerical MLP and head, then all parameters. Experiments merge 2,549 filtered Marin runs and 2,581 StepLaw runs, group configurations by (optimizer,N,D), assign groups at N <= 430M to an 80/20 train/ID split, and reserve all N > 430M groups for OOD evaluation. For HPO, the trained surrogate is queried over learning-rate and batch-size grids and a local quadratic fit refines the predicted minimum.
assumptions: A Chinchilla-style parameter-token law supplies the dominant trend outside the observed model scale, leaving a residual that is smoother and more transferable than raw loss.
Semantically related configuration names and values induce useful priors in a pretrained language model, especially when logs are heterogeneous and sparse.
A project/source identifier is an acceptable proxy for unrecorded differences in data, evaluation loss, model implementation, and training recipe.
Grouped splitting by (optimizer,N,D) prevents the most direct tuple leakage even though train and validation runs still come from the same projects and configuration families.
Filtered, completed, reasonably performing training runs are representative of the region in which the surrogate will be used.
The optimum of a smoothed/interpolated logged surface is a meaningful stand-in for the outcome of a prospective configuration trial.
Configuration effects learned at N <= 430M remain sufficiently stable up to roughly 1.2B parameters and higher token budgets.
A point prediction is adequate for optimization even without calibrated epistemic uncertainty or out-of-support detection.

techniques.role: Represents architecture, data scale, step, optimizer, schedule, and optimizer-specific fields in one variable-length sequence rather than a fixed hand-designed table.
Reuses a Qwen3-1.7B language-model backbone and attaches a scalar prediction head to its final-token representation.
Maps each scaled numeric value through a two-layer MLP so magnitudes are not fragmented into ordinary text tokens.
Fits a training-only best-run parameter-data law and asks the neural model to predict configuration-specific residuals, which supplies most of the measured OOD-scale stability.

Trains numerical embeddings and the output head first, then fine-tunes the full backbone; final-loss training uses 20 epochs at 5e-5 followed by 1,000 epochs at 1e-5 with AdamW, batch 480, and weight decay 0.01.
Keeps complete (optimizer,N,D) groups together, creates ID validation below the scale boundary, and uses every model above 430M parameters as OOD.
Adds current training step to the configuration so up to 30 checkpoints per run can supervise and query an entire loss curve.
Evaluates the learned surface across peak learning rate and batch size and locally fits a quadratic near its predicted minimum.
Excludes unfinished runs, losses above 4, runs more than 0.3 worse than the best at the same (N,D), and curves with a sufficiently positive local slope before modeling.

evaluations.result: 2,549 Marin plus 2,581 StepLaw runs survive filtering; 3,225 configurations train the model, 796 form ID validation, and 1,109 form OOD validation, with OOD reaching about 1.2B parameters and roughly 10x training compute.
evaluations.baseline: All groups at N <= 430M are eligible for the grouped 80/20 train/ID split; all N > 430M groups are OOD.

limitations: Author-stated (page 12): this is a proof of concept trained only through 430M parameters and evaluated only through about 1.2B, far below frontier-model scale.

Author-stated (pages 3 and 12): training configurations have limited diversity; Adam beta and epsilon values rarely vary, discrete hyperparameter grids leave unseen values unreliable, and the method cannot yet extrapolate to new architectures or datasets.
Author-stated (page 12): only dense Transformer runs from two public projects are studied; mixture-of-experts and linear-attention architectures are absent.

Reviewer-identified: the source tag absorbs unrecorded data-recipe and metric differences, so the experiment measures scale extrapolation within Marin and StepLaw, not transfer to an independent project or dataset.

Reviewer-identified: Marin evaluates English C4 validation loss while StepLaw supplies a smoothed training loss; separate baselines and a source token accommodate rather than resolve this target mismatch.
Reviewer-identified: logged optimizer and hyperparameter choices are observational and policy-confounded, so recovered interactions should not be interpreted as causal treatment effects.
Reviewer-identified: the OOD split changes model size and often token budget together, preventing clean attribution of error to parameter-scale versus data-scale extrapolation.

Reviewer-identified: point estimates have no seed intervals, predictive intervals, calibration test, support-distance diagnostic, or failure abstention, even though the model is proposed for optimization.

Reviewer-identified: the HPO comparison is retrospective and partly based on interpolated/smoothed logged surfaces; no selected configuration is prospectively trained and no aggregate simple regret or tuning cost is reported.
Reviewer-identified: filtering unfinished, unstable, and badly performing runs improves regression cleanliness but removes catastrophic regimes that a safe tuner most needs to recognize.
Reviewer-identified: the 1.7B backbone is not justified by an end-to-end cost/value comparison; on StepLaw a 135M scratch model and XGBoost are competitive or better on several metrics.

Reviewer-identified: 1,000 full-model fine-tuning epochs over a small corpus create an overfitting concern; grouped validation reduces exact tuple leakage but does not remove shared-project correlations.
failure_modes: The fitted Chinchilla anchor overpredicts a far-OOD run and the learned residual has the same sign, compounding rather than correcting error.
Training dominated by smaller models induces an excessively large learning-rate recommendation for the N=1.073B, D=57B case.
A new dataset or codebase has no valid source token, so unobserved recipe differences cannot be separated from configuration effects.
An unseen optimizer, architecture family, MoE routing scheme, attention mechanism, or numerical range falls outside the logged support while still receiving an unqualified point prediction.
The surrogate exploits interpolation error in the predicted surface and recommends a configuration whose prospectively trained loss is worse than the logged optimum.
A diverging or unstable run is classified outside the training distribution rather than assigned an appropriately catastrophic loss because such curves were filtered out.
Rarely varied Adam beta or epsilon fields appear syntactically supported but cannot have their effect learned from the corpus.
A source tag memorizes project-level offsets and creates good within-source test metrics without learning transferable configuration semantics.
Checkpoint losses near transient spikes or schedule transitions are poorly represented by the smooth residual model, especially on StepLaw where curve RMSE remains much larger than final-loss RMSE.
Fine-tuning a large pretrained backbone adds variance and cost on a simple regular corpus where the smaller scratch model is already superior.
reusable_insights: Factor a strong analytic scale trend from a flexible surrogate and audit the anchor and correction separately; an impressive OOD score may depend more on the analytic prior than on the neural learner.
Keep configuration groups intact across splits and reserve a scale axis for testing, but add independent-project and leave-one-family-out splits before claiming broad transfer.
Encode continuous magnitudes continuously even when the surrounding record is serialized as language; ordinary digit tokens discard useful numeric geometry.
Use full-configuration predictors to model systematic deviations from compute-optimal frontiers rather than replacing a well-supported scaling law outright.
Compare pretrained sequence models against small scratch and tabular models separately on heterogeneous and regular corpora; semantic pretraining is most plausible when schemas and regimes vary.
For tuning applications, validate selected points prospectively and report regret, cost, uncertainty calibration, and abstention—not only regression error over historical logs.
Preserve failed and unstable runs with an explicit failure target or classifier so a performance surrogate can support safe optimization.
Treat optimizer-by-hyperparameter surfaces learned from logs as hypotheses for randomized experiments, not as causal discoveries.
open_questions: Does NCPL transfer to an entirely held-out codebase and dataset when no source token from that project appears in training?
How much of the measured OOD advantage remains after replacing the neural model with a smaller residual MLP, Gaussian process, or boosted tree using the identical Chinchilla anchor?
Can calibrated ensembles or conformal intervals identify the far-scale learning-rate and residual-anchor failures before a configuration is trained?
What is the prospective simple regret and total compute cost when NCPL, StepLaw, XGBoost, and Bayesian optimization each select configurations under the same budget?
Can a factorized split isolate extrapolation in N, D, optimizer family, architecture, and numerical hyperparameter range one axis at a time?
Do semantic priors help with genuinely new configuration fields, or only with heterogeneity already correlated with project identity?
Can failed and divergent curves be incorporated through censored regression or a joint stability classifier without distorting the smooth-loss objective?
Does the method retain accuracy on MoE, recurrent/linear-attention, multimodal, and post-training workloads?
Would a jointly learned analytic trend outperform the fixed Chinchilla residual while avoiding the baseline-error compounding documented in Appendix B?
How sensitive are results to random seeds, group definitions, source balancing, and the 430M split threshold?

competitive_landscape.title: Predictable Scale: Part I, Step Law -- Optimal Hyperparameter Scaling Law in Large Language Model Pretraining
competitive_landscape.difference: StepLaw fits explicit learning-rate and batch-size power laws from 3,700 models and more than 100T training tokens, reporting a held-out choice 0.094% from exhaustive-search optimum and covering dense/MoE and multiple data recipes. NCPL consumes StepLaw logs as one of two corpora and generalizes to more configuration fields and whole curves, but only retrospectively matches StepLaw for learning-rate/batch-size tuning and is less interpretable.

competitive_landscape.title: Performance Prediction for Large Systems via Text-to-Text Regression
competitive_landscape.difference: This work already serializes system configurations for sequence-model regression and reports strong resource-prediction accuracy on Borg workloads, including predictive distributions. NCPL specializes the idea to language-model training, adds learned continuous-number tokens and a Chinchilla residual anchor, and evaluates scale OOD; its use of a pretrained 1.7B model is therefore an adaptation rather than the origin of text-to-text configuration regression.

competitive_landscape.title: Can Language Models Discover Scaling Laws?
competitive_landscape.difference: SLDAgent co-optimizes symbolic formulas and parameters over more than 5,000 experiments and eight tasks, returning interpretable analytic laws intended for extrapolation. NCPL directly regresses performance from a richer configuration sequence and does not emit a law; it can absorb categorical optimizer fields but offers less mechanistic interpretability and relies on a separately supplied analytic scale trend.

competitive_landscape.title: Tune My Adam, Please!
competitive_landscape.difference: Adam-PFN targets freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization, conditions on partial learning curves, models uncertainty, and is trained across TaskSet with OOD-task evaluation. NCPL covers more optimizer and architecture fields and predicts from pretraining configurations without requiring an observed partial curve, but lacks a sequential acquisition policy, calibrated uncertainty, and independent-task generalization.

competitive_landscape.title: How to Set the Learning Rate for Large-Scale Pre-training?
competitive_landscape.difference: This paper fits search-factor learning-rate scaling and extends transfer rules across depth, weight decay, token horizon, and MoE settings while examining why muTransfer can fail. NCPL models a broader black-box configuration-to-loss map, but its data are dense-model dominated and it supplies neither a mechanistic transfer account nor validated MoE coverage.

competitive_landscape.title: Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Porian et al. show that warmup, last-layer compute, and scale-dependent learning-rate/batch-size tuning reconcile conflicting compute-optimal laws and identify beta2 as important. NCPL learns losses for suboptimal full configurations, but its baseline inherits the Chinchilla functional form and its logs rarely vary several Adam fields, limiting what the neural residual can establish beyond that analytic prior.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper presents the first neural scaling law that maps a comprehensive heterogeneous pretraining configuration—not just model size and token count—to final performance and loss curves, using language-model priors to extrapolate and jointly optimize hyperparameters.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Across 5,130 filtered public runs from Marin and StepLaw, the full model improves over configuration-agnostic Chinchilla fits and, on the heterogeneous Marin corpus, over XGBoost and scratch backbones. It represents mixed categorical/numeric schemas and recovers optimizer-weight-decay and learning-rate/batch-size surfaces at held-out larger scales.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The credible increment is the combination of text-serialized heterogeneous pretraining configurations, continuous numeric embeddings, and a scaling-law residual for one reusable surrogate. Text-to-text configuration regression, analytic hyperparameter scaling, learned optimizers, and symbolic scaling-law discovery all predate it. Moreover, the residual ablation shows that the analytic Chinchilla anchor—not an unconstrained neural ansatz—provides most far-scale extrapolation, and the pretrained LLM advantage disappears on regular StepLaw data. Novelty is therefore moderate and engineering-compositional; claims of general configuration extrapolation remain unsupported outside two known dense-model projects.

The audit preserves three adverse results: reliance on the residual anchor, scratch/tabular wins on StepLaw, and the largest-scale learning-rate/baseline errors.
